Vigilante group

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How has an organised vigilante group called Mayitsha taken over a whole community in the Eastern Cape

Summary:
A group called Mayitsha started in 2017 with the idea that they would work with SAPS to curb crime in the Middledrift district (100km from East-London). But soon they took the law into their own hands, they felt that SAPS weren't doing enough and that criminals were simply being let out on bail.
So they started their own court with a council of 15 men who decide the fate of the accused, often not listening to both sides of the story. And then dishing out serious beatings inside the court as punishment

The chairman of Mayitsha is willing to speak to us and allow us to see a court proceeding. They have no fear of the police and feel they are within their rights, as the police do nothing to protect the community.

Mayitsha's leaders say that the community are thankful for their presence and the SAPS, as well as the Ward councillor, say that the community fear them

Two boys were killed in the court last year and their family will speak out openly
The Ward councillor is incredibly articulate and is willing to speak about the problems in the area and why this group was necessary in the beginning, but now they have become as bad as the criminals they were supposed to protect the community from
Captain Sozani from the police station that has been dealing with this group from the beginning will speak on behalf of the SAPS


Extra Budget Items:
Eastern Cape trip
100km from East-london to the village
Then the closest place to stay is 45 minute from where we will be shooting
Can get quotes tomorrow, as the interviews etc are all setup

Press Release:


Vigilante Justice
Against the backdrop of South Africa’s soaring crime rate and the outsourcing of safety and security to private companies in suburbia, Carte Blanche gets unprecedented access to the well-organised and notorious Mayitsha group that has become prosecutor, judge and executioner for anyone accused of crime in their Eastern Cape home village – and they claim a startling success rate. Research shows that 3% of South Africans belong to vigilante groups. Can this kind of outsourced justice restore the peace or will it further perpetuate division in a country where citizens are fed up with the high levels of violence.
Producer: Tarryn Crossman
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:















Time code Visual Character
00:00 Voice over According to the Numbero National crime index – south Africa is the 4th most dangerous country in the world. 56 people are murdered on a daily. South Africans are in a constant state of fear and many have lost faith in the police service to protect them. Giving rise to vigilante groups across the country
00:21 Macfarlane link Mayitsha an organized vigilante group operating in the Middledrift in the Eastern Cape, they have a council of 15 men who are judge, jury and executioner and they have been operating since 2017 largely untouched by the SAPS
00:36 Voice over We got an exclusive access to the inner working of this vigilante group. Welcome Nomtshatshu is a founding member of Mayitsha which was formed during the increase in crime in the area and a lack of police action. The nearest police station to the area is 25KM away.
00:54 Macfarlane and welcome interview Macfarlane: What were some of the things that were happening in the community that made you decide to start this group?

Welcome: An old lady was raped and killed by one of the young boys who stabbed her to death, we reported it and no response, this lady was killed by his boyfriend and we took the lady to the police but the law, the justice said there is not enough evidence and no one was arrested. Things are not good man we don’t have a choice because we want to protect our people e
01:24 Voice over When the mayitsha group started they were working with the police to handing over suspects but when there were no convictions they took the law into their own hands and started court system from this town hall were a councilor of 15 men questioned the accused and witnesses
01:39 Welcome The chairperson of mayitsha and his committee is standing and the chairperson of mayitsha is going to share the meeting. Anyone is allowed to come and any one is allowed to ask question if you got a question
01:52 Voice over When court is in session a whistle is blown for the community to attend. Once the proceedings are finished the punishment is decided by the council of 15.
02:02 Macfarlane and Welcome Macfarlane: What kind of punishment is given to people that are found guilty by the group?

Welcome: Our law is we don’t use knifes, we don’t use panga, we don’t use guns. If you use it to stab someone then we don’t discuss anything with you we just give you a lash

Macfarlane: Who decided on this punishment?
Welcome: All of us as a group
02:23 Welcome at the hall A person found guilty they lie here and then we do the lashes. So if there are 15t guys each and everyone just one lash one lash and then you are finished
02:34 Voice over In South Africa 3% of the population belong to some form of a vigilante group and this rises to 5% in the eastern Cape.
Lizette Lancaster is the manager for the Crime and Justice information hub and the Institute for security Studies.
02:50 Lizette All south Africans feel vulnerable, we know that 80% of people do not feel safe walking in the areas during after dark but of course if you are in suburbia and you can afford and you met law enforcement and private security services or you put up high walls or you have burglar proofing and you have alarm systems. However if with adverse poverty, no services and high crime rate then of course your options are limited to safe guard yourself. And it is extremely difficult not to take the law into your own hands sometimes when your family lives or your property is threatened.
03:34 Voice over Brigadier Thembisle Kenana is the Eastern Cape spokesperson for the south Africa police services
03:40 B. Kinana We do understand that people get frustrated sometimes, you remember with incidence happening in their community. But we discourage people taking the law into their own hands there a process, there are structures that people must actually follow in order to get their complaints attend to
04:02 Voice over In November last year, Sithembele was dragged into the Mayitsha court room following a family dispute and found guilty for using a weapon even though he denies this
04:13 Sithembele interview with Macfarlane Sithembele: It was a shock that I was called to the hall. They said that I beat up my brother and I used a weapon. I said I didn’t use a weapon
04:24 Welcome Only thing make us to be involved in that matter is because Sithembele was having a weapon
04:32 Sithembele They Sjambok us, sjambok us, sjambok us and the hall was full. So everyone at the hall sjambokked me with 2 whips

Macfarlane: everyone in the hall?

Sithembele: Everyone in the hall
04:49 Lizette These groups are formed out of desperation and potent there is great support for them in these communities and often the evidence suggests that crime plummets in these areas because of patrols by these groups and intervention but as with all group type activity is extremely difficult to control the actions of the group. Vigilante type of activity can often turn ordinary people that just want order in their areas into violent criminals
05:22 Voice over Fezeka Mgqwannci son Bantu was apprehended by Mayitsha and accused of rape and murder
05:29 Fezeka interview with MacFarlane They took him to the hall and that’s when he was sjambokked. After they sjambokked him he never came back. They killed him at the river. They’d killed him like a dog. My son was killed like a dog
05:42 Voice over Since mayitsha started in 2017 they have allegally been 3 incidences where the punishment escalated from sjambok to murder and was the case with Bantu
05:53 MacFarlane and Welcome Macfarlane: Was it the community or was it members of the mayitsha group that eventually led to this guy’s death

Welcome: No it’s the members of mayitsha and not the community.

Macfarlane: Do you regret what happened?
Welcome: yes, we don’t want those things happen, the intent is to make the person know what they done is wrong and they must stop it. To go to someone death is not our aim at all
MacFarlane: have you ever tried to communicate to the family to maybe apologies?
Welcome: yes, I did as a… because that time I was a chair person

MacFarlane: Has anyone ever been arrested or what’s sort of just should then be given to someone who is now done that?
Welcome: no there is nothing happened after that.
06:35 Voice over q No arrests have been made with regards to Bantus murder which took place in 2017 but 5 members have been charged with assault for what happened to Sithembele they are currently out on bail
06:48 B. Kinanan You know this group you have this tendency of intimidating everybody within the community that no body must talk to the police, nobody must give information to the police and we would find ourselves being accused of having dragged cases or not making break through only to find its because you know challenges that we are trying to you know address
07:15 Fezeka Fezeka: it’s painful, we vote in south Africa because we need help and we’re meant to get it. The police are actually where we go last to get help.
07:32 MacFarlane and Welcome Macfarlane: Welcome how sure are you that every time somebody appears before you get it right?

Welcome: at the moment all the people that we find guilty we have spotted on, no one can say I wasn’t doing anything but I was punished
07:49 Lizette These groups are acting as the police, the prosecution authority views, the court the department of justice as well as the prison services. It is fast but often very inaccurate justice
08:09 MacFarlane and Welcome Macfarlane: Do you believe you have made a difference in your community?
Welcome: Yes, I do believe

MacFarlane: how?
Welcome: before this group you can’t walk after 8. Before this group there were so many house break, the rape today you can sleep without closing the door, no one will come each and every one is involved
08:34 Macfarlane Link Daily South Africans are faced with a tough question of how far would you go to protect your loved ones? Has this group c=gone too far or are they doing just what they can to stay safe?
08:46 Lizette This country is formed on violence, every time a new colonial took over land it was with violence so it’s not new to us but I think we are not winning the battle against getting to alternative to violence for negotiating conflicts
09:07 Voice over Fearing for his safety Sithembele has been removed from the village and placed in witness protection by the SAPS
09:13 Macfarlane with Sithembele MacFarlane: do you still want to go back home?
Sithembele: Very Much, even now if they had to say I could go I would go. It’s my home
Macfarlane: But your scared to go back?
Sithembele: I’m scared because those people could kill me
09:28 Lizette You know violence as a social norm doesn’t just act in certain communities it’s in all of us so as much as people hate the violence that happen, hate that crime that occur they are very quick to act in a violent way and the thing is that we all then start accepting violence as a tool to fight violence and I do not know where that will leave our children one day
